To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the brain changes that occur in the transition from healthy aging to AD are subtle and difficult to detect; 2) there is a growing body of evidence for divergence of brain changes that may distinguish between healthy aging and incipient AD; and 3) the evidence for this divergence comes from a variety of research methods, but the most promising findings come from longitudinal studies of individuals who are at risk for AD due to genetic or lifestyle factors.
there are differences in cognitive and structural brain measures that may distinguish healthy aging from AD-related changes in asymptomatic middle-aged adults.

the cognitive changes that differentiate healthy aging from the incipient AD process are subtle and include a decline in memory performance, a reduction in the ability to learn and retain new information, a decline in the ability to switch between tasks and to inhibit prepotent responses, and an increase in the ability to detect and respond to errors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the earliest stages of AD and identifying biomarkers of incipient disease processes in midlife.
the question: Can we identify, in midlife, individuals who will remain cognitively healthy throughout life, and those who will develop dementia?
the early identification of AD and the development of strategies to delay its onset.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no clear evidence that midlife cognitive and structural brain markers are useful in distinguishing between healthy aging and pathological aging.
the evidence for divergence between the trajectories of healthy aging and dementia from midlife is mixed, and the evidence for the presence of early biomarkers of dementia is weak.
there is a need for further research to better define the early stages of AD-related pathology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the future, we should be able to identify people who are at risk of developing AD in midlife.
the cognitive and neuroanatomical changes that differentiate healthy aging and dementia in midlife are subtle, and that they do not appear to be present at the same time.
the brain changes associated with the incipient stages of AD-related pathology may be detected in the midlife period and are distinguishable from those associated with typical healthy aging.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the midlife period may be a critical window to intervene and prevent the onset of dementia.

the midlife period may be an ideal time to intervene to reduce the risk of AD, and that a more comprehensive understanding of the early stages of the disease is necessary to identify the most promising targets for prevention and intervention.

the cognitive and structural brain signatures of healthy aging and AD-related processes begin to diverge from midlife, and the earlier these divergences are detected, the better the prognosis for the prevention and treatment of AD.
